speakers: Campbell R. Harvey (Duke University; Man Group)
summary: Do carry, momentum and value work better as directional (time-series) or cross-asset implementations? Daily backtest 1990-Apr 2015 of 87 futures/forwards/swaps across equity, rates, FX and commodities, with theory review for each style. Value is a cross-sectional style, momentum a time-series style, carry works in both; combining styles and implementations reaches Sharpe about 1.6 gross of costs.

coverage.note: carry definition, Jensen forward bias, arbitrage forward
CAPM forward bias, dividend factor, Lustig-Verdelhan
carry theories by asset class, momentum definition
momentum theories, disposition model, value definition
value in rates and equities (consumption model, Gordon)
overshooting, value stories, data, FX carry formula
momentum normalisation, response function, value formulas
swap value, CS and TS portfolio construction, 15% vol
FX slow rebalancing, CS single-style results Table 1
Table 1C, Table 2 correlations, commodity inventory logic
Table 3 betas, Table 4 combined CS, Figure 1
Table 5 TS results, equity value, carry-momentum correlation
Figures 7-8, monthly/linear robustness, CS vs TS core findings
explanations of CS vs TS difference
commodity and rates universe, start dates

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: we offer some insights on the market conditions that favor the application of a particular setting
claims.claim: The paper compares carry, momentum and value implemented directionally (time series) versus across assets (cross section) to learn which market conditions favour which setting.
claims.testable: partly - framed as insights, not a single test

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: momentum is almost always traded across assets (relative value) whereas in futures trading, momentum is typically applied directionally. Why?
claims.claim: Practice differs: cash equity momentum is traded cross-sectionally, futures momentum directionally; the authors ask why and test both implementations.
claims.testable: partly - motivates the cross-section vs time-series comparison

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: if the market factor is trending, then it is more likely time-series momentum will be profitable than cross-sectional momentum
claims.claim: If the dominant market factor is trending, time-series (directional) momentum should beat cross-sectional momentum, because a market-neutral cross-sectional book hedges out that factor.
claims.direction: TS momentum > CS momentum when global factor trends
claims.conditions: works when the first principal component (market/global factor) trends; if predictability sits in the other factors the cross-sectional form is preferred
claims.testable: yes - compare TS vs CS momentum against global-factor trendiness

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We fill this gap by providing an analysis of both the time- series and cross-section using a broad number of asset classes: equity, fixed income, currencies and commodities.
claims.claim: Scope: carry, value and momentum tested both ways in four asset classes (equity, fixed income, currency, commodity), plus combined time-series and cross-sectional information.
claims.data_needed: equity index futures, rate swaps, FX, commodity futures

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: we are testing three strategies that are select - they are popular because they have worked.
claims.claim: The three styles were selected because they are known to have worked, so positive average returns are partly a selection effect; the aim is to understand conditions, not to find the most profitable strategy.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Important drivers are the correlation of asset returns, the correlation of the information that drives markets
claims.claim: The difference between directional and cross-asset performance is driven by correlation of asset returns, correlation of the underlying (partly unobservable) information, and correlation of trading signals; to be explored in a future paper.
claims.testable: partly - drivers named but not tested here

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: these strategies are largely profitable over our sample - and the best performance is when these strategies are combined
claims.claim: Headline: the three styles are largely profitable and the combination of styles performs best.
claims.reported_result: qualitative; see Tables 1-12

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We define carry as the difference between the spot and the forward price of an asset
claims.claim: Carry is spot minus forward, i.e. the profit on a long forward position if prices do not change.
claims.exact_rule: carry = spot - forward (profit on a long forward if spot unchanged)

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: buying the asset forward if the carry is positive or selling it forward if the carry is negative
claims.claim: Simple carry trade: go long the forward when carry is positive, short when negative.
claims.exact_rule: position sign = sign(carry); long forward if carry>0, short if carry<0
claims.direction: long if carry>0, short if carry<0

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: This means that forward prices cannot be unbiased predictors of future spot prices.
claims.claim: By Jensen's inequality (F=E(S) for A per B and for B per A cannot both hold), forwards cannot be unbiased predictors of future spot, so a systematic forward bias must exist in all asset classes; for FX this means uncovered interest parity cannot hold.
claims.testable: no - theoretical argument; empirical size tested via carry returns

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: By standard arbitrage, the forward price is equal to the spot price compounded at the risk-free rate minus the dividend yield
claims.claim: Forward = spot * exp((r-d)(T-t)), so carry on a dividend-paying asset is positive when the risk-free rate exceeds the dividend yield.
claims.exact_rule: F(t,T)=S(t)*exp((r-d)(T-t)); eq. (4)

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Note that the carry is positive (negative) if the interest rate is greater (smaller) than the dividend yield.
claims.claim: Sign of carry = sign(r - d).

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: If the asset beta is positive as is generally the case, the forward price is lower than the expected spot price
claims.claim: Under CAPM, E(S_T)=S_t exp((r+beta*pi-d)(T-t)); for positive-beta assets the forward is below expected spot, so a long forward earns expected P&L S_t e^{(r-d)(T-t)}[e^{beta*pi(T-t)}-1] > 0 (systematic forward bias).
claims.testable: partly - needs beta and equity risk premium

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: The sign of the forward bias is independent of carry
claims.claim: In plain CAPM the forward bias depends on beta*pi, not on r-d, so carry as a signal has no explanation from the market factor alone.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: The higher the dividend yield, the higher the carry, the lower the forward compared to the expected spot price, the more profitable the carry trade.
claims.claim: With a dividend (value-proxy) factor in expected returns, forward bias correlates with carry: higher yield means higher carry and a more profitable carry trade.
claims.conditions: requires an asset pricing model richer than CAPM (dividend factor loading gamma)

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: high-yielding currencies tend to depreciate whereas low-yielding currencies hold their own in low domestic consumption states
claims.claim: Citation (Lustig and Verdelhan 2007): low-yielding currencies hedge low domestic consumption states and so carry lower expected returns than high yielders, a risk-based reason for FX carry.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: find the strategy is rela- tively uncorrelated with factors such as value and momentum but is partially explained by recession and volatility risk
claims.claim: Citation (Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen, Vrugt 2013): carry across asset classes is relatively uncorrelated with value and momentum but partly explained by recession and volatility risk.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: This trade can be profitable because high-yields are associated with non-diversifiable risk factors such as political turmoil or wavering property rights
claims.claim: FX carry (buy high-yield, sell low-yield currency) is compensation for non-diversifiable risks (political turmoil, weak property rights, persistent inflation).

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: the yield differential can remunerate a so-called peso effect, meaning that jump risk can be very real even though it has not materialized
claims.claim: The yield differential can pay for peso-problem jump risk that has not materialised in the sample, so realised carry returns may overstate safety.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: a high yield on a currency can reflect a central bank just about to gain or regain anti-inflation
claims.claim: Alternative reading: a high yield can reflect a central bank about to (re)establish anti-inflation credibility that will make the currency more desirable.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: was interpreted by Keynes as the result of producers selling futures to insure themselves against price falls
claims.claim: Normal backwardation (Keynes): producers sell futures for insurance, creating structural excess futures supply so curves are backwardated and futures roll up to spot.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: But as observed empirically, backwardation is not the norm, particularly today.
claims.claim: Empirically commodity curves are often not backwardated, so the Keynesian insurance story is incomplete.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: speculators are incented by hedgers to sell contangoed futures and buy backwardated futures
claims.claim: Hedgers can be on either side (airlines are naturally long futures), so contango can pay speculators to be short; speculators earn carry by buying backwardation and selling contango.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: the theory of storage links backwardation to tight inventories
claims.claim: Theory of storage (Working 1933, Kaldor 1939, Schwartz 1997): low inventories give a high convenience yield, hence backwardation; inventories rebuild slowly so carry profits can persist.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Rates tend to roll down the curve: this translates into excess returns for fixed income investors.
claims.claim: Fixed income carry is roll-down on an upward-sloping curve (liquidity premium / preferred habitat explanations), giving excess returns.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: The conventional trade (at least for academic purposes) is to buy assets that outperformed and sell assets that underperformed over the previous year.
claims.claim: Conventional momentum: buy past 12-month winners, sell losers.
claims.exact_rule: long assets with high prior-12m return, short low

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: the sweet spot for momentum, or positively auto-correlated, strategies is around 6-12 months
claims.claim: Returns show negative autocorrelation below one month and above three years; positive autocorrelation (momentum sweet spot) is at 6-12 months.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Theories of momentum range from the risk-based to the behavioral.
claims.claim: Momentum explanations are split between risk-based (sensitivity to macro factors) and behavioural (underreaction/overreaction).

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: growth rate of industrial production (Liu and Zhang, 2008)
claims.claim: Risk story: high-momentum assets are more sensitive to macro factors such as industrial production growth (Liu and Zhang 2008).

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: a cross-section of past winners with high realized returns has higher expected returns and ends up outperforming a cross-section of past losers
claims.claim: Conrad and Kaul (1988): when realised and expected returns are highly correlated, past winners have higher expected returns and outperform past losers.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: investors underreact to news either because they display conservatism bias and are slow updating their beliefs
claims.claim: Behavioural: underreaction from conservatism (Barberis, Shleifer, Vishny 1998) or asynchronous information receipt (Hong and Stein 1999) produces momentum.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: prices can overreact to news and feed upon themselves with noise traders deepening the mis-pricing
claims.claim: Alternative: prices overreact and feed on themselves via noise traders, deepening mispricing until a reversal.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: behavioral biases can generate momentum when fund flows exhibit inertia and the market under-reacts to expected future flows
claims.claim: Vayanos and Woolley (2013): fund-flow inertia and under-reaction to expected flows generate persistence until a large deviation from fundamentals triggers reversal.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Investors tend to sell their winning stocks too early while holding on to their losers.
claims.claim: Disposition effect (Grinblatt and Han 2002): with rational fraction mu and disposition fraction 1-mu, equilibrium price P_t = w F_t + (1-w) P_{t-1} with w=1/(1+mu*alpha), so price is positively correlated with yesterday's price and only partially reflects fundamentals.
claims.exact_rule: P_t = w*F_t + (1-w)*P_{t-1}, w = 1/(1+mu*alpha)

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Behavioral biases, combined with more liquid markets and more efficient information diffusion, tend to favor persistence of slow momentum.
claims.claim: Authors' view (AHL/MSS board): unprecedented policy (negative rates, QE, wealth-effect focus) makes investors rely on heuristics and anchoring, which together with liquid markets favours persistence of slow momentum; 'qualified yes' that momentum is behavioural in today's markets.
claims.testable: partly - regime claim for post-2008 policy era

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Value can be defined as the difference between a fundamental asset price and its prevailing market price.
claims.claim: Value = fundamental price minus market price; the paper discusses fundamental measures for rates, stocks, currencies and commodities.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: we can solve for the equilibrium real interest rate
claims.claim: Value for rates: with log utility and lognormal consumption the equilibrium real rate is r = g + rho - sigma^2 (deterministic r = g), so real rates are anchored by consumption growth.
claims.exact_rule: r = g + rho - sigma^2 (log utility); r = g (deterministic); CRRA: r = gamma*g + rho - gamma^2 sigma^2/2 per footnote 2

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: When capital is free to move across countries, there is evidently a tendency for real rates of return to converge.
claims.claim: Value for rates can also be the domestic-foreign real-rate differential: higher domestic real rates create excess demand for domestic bonds.
claims.direction: long markets with high real rates vs foreign

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: the equity yield is the sum of the dividend growth and the dividend yield
claims.claim: Gordon: P = D/(R-g_d); implied equity yield R = g + D/P; implied ERP = g - r + D/P, which with r=g reduces to ERP = D/P, justifying the dividend yield as equity value measure.
claims.exact_rule: R = g + D/P; ERP = R - r = g - r + D/P; if r=g then ERP = D/P

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Dividend yields can therefore be used as a measure of value for broad equity markets.
claims.claim: Equity index value measure = dividend yield (high yield = cheap versus bonds).

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Of course the dividend yield can be time-varying and thus not necessarily a measure of value.
claims.claim: Caveat: dividend yield is time-varying and, when rates are below growth, understates the equity risk premium; leverage may also mean the ERP is less than it looks.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: high price-to-book ratios are a presumption of expensiveness.
claims.claim: Alternative equity value measures: price-to-book and Tobin's Q (market cap over replacement cost; Q>1 means expensive).

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: high (low) commodity prices incentivise producers to boost (reduce) supply which in turn results in downward (upward) pressure on prices
claims.claim: Commodity value works because high prices stimulate supply and low prices reduce it, and competitive prices gravitate to production cost; value is a bet on long mean-reversion cycles.
claims.direction: short expensive / long cheap commodity vs history

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: purchasing power parity (PPP) has the most intuitive appeal
claims.claim: Currency value = deviation of real exchange rate from PPP; frictions (transport, tariffs, sticky prices, capital flows, policy) cause deviations; the authors call PPP 'more a tautology than a theory'.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Dornbusch's overshooting model (1976) is an example of a rational story that explains large deviations from PPP.
claims.claim: Dornbusch overshooting: with sticky goods prices, flexible asset prices, UIP and PPP long run, an unanticipated money supply increase lowers the domestic rate so the currency must depreciate beyond PPP, then appreciates back.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: While this model is arbitrage free - the value premium is perfectly neutralized by the carry
claims.claim: In the Dornbusch model value premium is offset by carry (no free lunch), but overshooting still creates value opportunities in assets that adjust slowly (e.g. euro real estate after the euro depreciation).

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: attribute the out-performance of value portfolios (relative to growth portfolios) to a higher long term exposure to consumption risk
claims.claim: Citation (Hansen, Heaton, Li): value outperformance reflects higher long-run consumption risk exposure (risk-based story).

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: value strategies outperform glamour strategies because investors put excessive weight on past history
claims.claim: Behavioural value stories: extrapolation of past history (Lakonishok, Shleifer, Vishny 1994); prospect-theory/myopic loss aversion (Benartzi and Thaler); ambiguity aversion (Maenhout 1999) partly explaining the equity premium.

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: The sample period starts in January 1990 and ends in April 2015.
claims.claim: Sample Jan 1990 - Apr 2015; sources Bloomberg, Global Financial Data, Man-AHL proprietary database.
claims.data_needed: Bloomberg, Global Financial Data, Man-AHL database

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We study 26 equity futures markets, 14 interest rate swap contracts, 31 currency pairs, and 16 commodity futures.
claims.claim: Universe: 26 equity futures, 14 interest-rate swaps, 31 currency pairs (versus USD), 16 commodity futures; all prices in USD.
claims.exact_rule: universe 26 EQ / 14 IR swaps / 31 FX / 16 commodities; USD prices

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We used mid-market prices and do not therefore account for trading costs
claims.claim: All results use mid prices with no trading costs, so reported Sharpe ratios are gross of costs (daily rebalancing makes this material).

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We used the 3 month FX-forward to imply the carry
claims.claim: FX carry = 4 x (Spot/Fwd_3M - 1), annualised from the 3-month forward.
claims.exact_rule: Carry_t = 4*(Spot_t / Fwd3M_t - 1)

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We used the first two futures of each index and computed a raw carry signal as follows
claims.claim: Equity carry raw signal = (Fut_T1 - Fut_T2)/Fut_T2 * 1/(T2-T1) from the first two index futures.
claims.exact_rule: RawCarry_t = [1/(T2-T1)] * (Fut_{t,T1} - Fut_{t,T2}) / Fut_{t,T2}
claims.data_needed: first and second index futures prices and expiries

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: For every month m, we compute a seasonality adjustment which is the average difference between the raw carry and its 1Y moving average
claims.claim: Equity carry is seasonally adjusted: subtract, for each calendar month m, the average (to date) of raw carry minus its 1Y moving average over all past days in month m (dividend seasonality).
claims.exact_rule: Adj_t = average over past days in same calendar month of [RawCarry - 1Y MA(RawCarry)]; Carry_t = RawCarry_t - Adj_t
claims.conditions: expanding sample: only data up to t

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: we used the first future and the contract exactly expiring one year later
claims.claim: Commodity carry uses the first future against the contract expiring exactly one year later to remove seasonality: Carry = (Fut_{T1+1y} - Fut_{T1})/Fut_{T1+1y}.
claims.exact_rule: Carry_t = (Fut_{t,T1+1} - Fut_{t,T1}) / Fut_{t,T1+1}, T1+1 = one year after T1

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Carry is meant as ”carry + roll down”.
claims.claim: Swap carry = (S10Y - Fixing)/Duration + (S10Y - S7Y)/3 i.e. carry plus roll-down, with modified duration (1-(1+S10Y)^-10)/S10Y.
claims.exact_rule: Carry_t = (S_10Y,t - Fixing_t)/Duration_t + (S_10Y,t - S_7Y,t)/3; Duration_t = (1-(1+S_10Y,t)^-10)/S_10Y,t

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: For all asset classes, we used a CTA-momentum signal, based on the cross over of exponentially weighted moving averages.
claims.claim: Momentum for every asset class is a CTA-style multi-speed EWMA crossover signal; speeds S_k=(8,16,32) and L_k=(24,48,96), each n converted to lambda=(n-1)/n, half-life log(0.5)/log(1-1/n).
claims.exact_rule: three pairs EWMA(P|S_k)-EWMA(P|L_k), S=(8,16,32), L=(24,48,96); lambda=(n-1)/n; HL=log0.5/log(1-1/n)

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We normalize with a moving standard deviation as a measure of the realized 3-months normal volatility (PW=63)
claims.claim: Each crossover x_k is divided by 63-day running standard deviation of price, then standardised again by the running 252-day standard deviation of y_k.
claims.exact_rule: x_k=EWMA(P|S_k)-EWMA(P|L_k); y_k=x_k/RunStDev(P,63); z_k=y_k/RunStDev(y_k,252)

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: The final CTA momentum signal is the weighted sum of the intermediate signals
claims.claim: Response function R(x)=x*exp(-x^2/4)/0.89 dampens extreme signals; u_k=R(z_k); final signal is equal-weighted (1/3) sum of u_k.
claims.exact_rule: u_k=R(z_k), R(x)=x*exp(-x^2/4)/0.89; S_CTA = (1/3)*sum_k u_k
claims.conditions: response function caps position as signal grows; reduces exposure to extreme trends

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We used relative PPP (purchasing power parity) as value indicator
claims.claim: FX value = log of CPI-adjusted real spot minus its long-run (historical) mean; real spot = spot x CPI_1/CPI_2.
claims.exact_rule: Value_t = log(SpotReal_t) - mean(log(SpotReal)); SpotReal = Spot_CCY1/CCY2 * CPI_CCY1/CPI_CCY2
claims.testable: partly - averaging window of 'overbar' not specified

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We used dividend yield as value indicator
claims.claim: Equity value signal = index dividend yield.
claims.exact_rule: Value_t = DivYield_t

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Value is defined as today’s deflated price divided by the deflated historical average price
claims.claim: Commodity value = US-CPI-deflated price divided by the deflated expanding-window average of all prices; sign is long when ratio is low.
claims.exact_rule: Value_t = AdjPrice_t / mean(AdjPrice over expanding window); AdjPrice=Price/US_CPI

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We defined value, in the rate space, as the difference between the 10Y swap rate and the most recent nominal GDP growth rate
claims.claim: Rates value = 10Y swap rate minus latest nominal GDP growth (quarterly, lagged 3 months); results with CPI inflation instead were quite similar.
claims.exact_rule: Value_t = S_10Y,t - NominalGDPgrowth_t (3-month lag)
claims.indicator: 10Y swap rate minus nominal GDP growth

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: We tested both definitions and the results were quite similar.
claims.claim: Replacing nominal GDP growth with y/y CPI inflation in rates value gave similar results; GDP version is used throughout.
claims.reported_result: 'quite similar' (numbers not shown)

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: we ranked all the assets according to the magnitude of the signal and took long/short positions on the six most extreme assets (three on each side)
claims.claim: Cross-sectional portfolio: per style and asset class, rank assets by signal, long top 3 and short bottom 3, equal risk weights regardless of signal size, rebalanced every trading day.
claims.exact_rule: rank by signal; long 3 highest, short 3 lowest; equal risk per position; daily rebalance

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: Afterwards, we tested for other configurations and the results were compa- rable
claims.claim: Using other numbers of extreme assets than six gave comparable results (footnote 5).
claims.reported_result: 'comparable' (numbers not shown)

claims.speaker: Jamil Baz; Nick Granger; Campbell R. Harvey; Nicolas Le Roux; Sandy Rattray
claims.quote: we computed the ex-ante volatility of each of the portfolios and scaled their allocations for an annualized volatility of 15% per portfolio
claims.claim: Aggregating asset classes: each portfolio is scaled ex ante to 15% annualised vol; aggregating styles uses equal weights because vol comes mostly from asset class choice.
claims.exact_rule: scale each asset-class portfolio to 15% ex-ante annual vol; equal weight across styles

reasoning.question: Should carry, momentum and value be traded directionally (time series) or cross-asset (long-short), and which market conditions decide? It matters because the choice changes net market exposure, which factor risks are hedged and how much of each signal's information is kept.

thesis.statement: Value works best cross-sectionally, momentum best directionally and carry in both; a cross-sectional book is a time-series book with the global factor hedged out, so the right choice depends on whether the global factor trends or mean-reverts and on how correlated signals are relative to assets. All versions combined give high but selection-biased, gross-of-cost Sharpe ratios.

foundations.premise: Forward prices are biased predictors of future spot (Jensen; CAPM forward bias), so a carry premium can exist; with a dividend/value factor the bias is tied to carry.
Carry premia compensate non-diversifiable risks (crash/peso risk in FX, recession and volatility risk) or hedging pressure and inventories in commodities and term premia in rates.
foundations.support: citations (Lustig-Verdelhan, Koijen et al., Keynes, theory of storage)

foundations.premise: Returns persist at 6-12 months and reverse at very short and multi-year horizons; momentum comes from underreaction, flow inertia or disposition effects (or risk exposure).
Asset prices revert toward fundamental anchors (real rate ~ growth, dividend yield ~ ERP, PPP, production cost), slowly, after overshooting.
foundations.support: consumption model, Gordon model, PPP, Dornbusch

foundations.premise: Within an asset class there is a dominant global (market) factor; a market-neutral long-short book hedges it out.
foundations.support: PCA intuition; algebra for linear signals

foundations.premise: Few investors can sit through multi-year underperformance, so simple premia are not arbitraged away.

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs: (1) carry (forward premium, futures slope, swap carry+roll) leads returns over months via risk-premium/forward-bias step; (2) EWMA-crossover trend leads over weeks-months via slow reaction; (3) value anchors (PPP gap, DY, real price vs history, 10Y minus nominal GDP) lead over years via mean reversion. For the CS vs TS choice: the autocorrelation/trend of the asset-class average return and the ratio of average signal correlation to average asset correlation should predict which implementation wins. These stop working if the global factor flips from trending to mean-reverting (hurting TS momentum, helping TS value), if crowding removes the patience premium, or if costs from daily binary rebalancing eat the gross edge.
reader_inferences: (reader) The TS value result likely depends on how the always-positive value signals were centred, which the paper does not state; a demeaned or z-scored version could behave differently.
(reader) The 2015 sample includes a 30-year bond rally and equity bull market, so the TS momentum vs value gap may be regime-specific rather than structural.
(reader) The commodity carry sign as printed would invert the trade; real implementation must have used backwardation-positive carry given the positive commodity carry Sharpe.
(reader) The 'close to 2' Sharpe in Section 5 is probably rhetorical or from an unreported variant; 1.61 is the documented figure.

(reader) Since CS+TS = TS minus half the global mean, a continuous hedge ratio on the global factor (0 to 1) chosen by the global factor's autocorrelation is the natural generalisation the paper points to.
